lines.text: Interviewer: Good morning, Sally.
Thank you for joining us today.
My first question might be an obvious one.
What are GM foods?
Food scientist: Well, as some of you may know, GM foods are plants, like corn, rice, bananas and many more, which have been changed by scientists in a way that does not occur in nature.
For example, in simple terms, if a scientist wants to make red bananas, they can get a red plant, cut out a piece of it that carries the information for red colour and insert it into the banana.
They then plant the new banana seed and the tree will produce red bananas instead of yellow.
Interviewer: Wow, that sounds amazing!
But are these foods good for us?
Food scientist: Well, that’s a difficult question to answer.
GM foods have been changed by scientists, but, despite what some people claim, there’s no evidence that they are actually bad for us to eat.
People have been trying to find a way to end world hunger for many years and GM foods may be part of the solution – they could feed millions of people around the world.
Interviewer: Can you tell us more about why scientists make these changes to plants?
Food scientist: Well, sometimes for health reasons.
For instance, changes like these can be used to increase the amount of vitamins in a food.
In one project, food scientists made changes to rice so that it contained more vitamin A and was healthier than ordinary rice.
This ‘healthy’ rice was then sent to countries where people had poor diets and were getting sick.
Interviewer: Is that the only reason food is changed?
Food scientist: No, there are a number of reasons.
For example, scientists can make certain vegetables, like tomatoes, grow bigger.
Also, in areas where agriculture can be challenging, farmers can use these changed plants to grow foods in bad conditions that are not typically suitable for growing crops.
This is extremely helpful in countries that are very dry or have little rain.
Interviewer: That’s interesting.

Food scientist: It is, and these days this type of produce is becoming even more critical, as farming conditions are expected to get worse in many areas due to the effects of rising temperatures and climate change.
Interviewer: Absolutely!
Are these crops more expensive to produce?
Food scientist: Well, that’s an interesting question.
Generally, production costs are lower because farmers do not need to use expensive chemicals.
This is because scientists can improve the quality of the crop so that it fights diseases, which means that these plants can protect themselves from bugs and other pests that normally harm it.

Recently, however, some scientists who have investigated the relationship between these foods and disease argue that crops may need more chemicals, because, as the crop gets stronger, the bugs and pests do, too.
So you see, some scientists support this process, whilst others remain a bit doubtful about the long-term effects as these still remain unknown.
Interviewer: What about the farmers themselves?
Does anything change for them?
Food scientist: Well, yes.

Agricultural crops can become the property of a private company, which means that the company, often a large multinational one, owns the crop and therefore decides what can and cannot be done with it.
This can have a negative effect on the farmers.
Interviewer: How so?
Food scientist: OK, so normally farmers keep some seeds from their current crop when it is harvested.
They do this so they can plant the seeds the following year.
Obviously, this saves money as the farmer doesn’t need to buy the seeds they are going to plant.
But if, for example, a company owns the crop and can make all the farming decisions, that company may require farmers to purchase new seeds from them.
Of course, this might mean the farmers’ costs increase and their profits decrease.
Interviewer: I see.
It’s not straightforward, is it?
Right thank you for joining us today, Sally.
I’m afraid that’s all we have time for.
And now, for something a little different.

lines.text: Tom: Hey, Sienna, I’m glad I’ve seen you.
Do you have a moment?
Sienna: Hi, Tom.
Yeah, sure.
Tom: Great.
I wanted to get your opinion on the changes happening at the hospital before this afternoon’s meeting.
You know, the decision that doing more clinical trials is necessary.
Sienna: Ah, yes.
Tom: How do you feel about the changes?
Sienna: Well, you are right that this research is necessary, but as I see it, there are more important things to focus on first, like making improvements to our working conditions.
Tom: Yes, working conditions could definitely be improved, but to me the data that’s collected by researchers from clinical trials is very valuable.
Otherwise we wouldn’t know if new treatments are safe or effective.
Sienna: So, what do you think are the key things that we need to focus on?
Tom: Well, there’s a lot of work to do around patient understanding.
From my perspective, some patients do not agree to take part in trials because they don’t know what treatments are available.
We need to make sure that we discuss all treatment options with our patients.
Sienna:Hmm, OK, Tom, but it seems to me that in addition to discussing options we need to make sure that patients know what is expected of them if they take part in a trial.
Tom: Yes, I agree.
What about support for us, the doctors?
Sienna: Well, we need more information and support, too.
I have had this experience myself at another hospital.
Although the process itself isn’t too complex, completing the extra paperwork takes too much time.
As you know, when a patient takes part in a clinical trial, there are a lot of extra appointments that wouldn’t be necessary if the patients were offered a standard treatment.
To be honest, I’m really not sure we have the time for that.
Tom: Of course time is a problem, but it seems to me that the additional training we are going to receive will help us understand how to complete the extra forms and documents.
Sienna: I think it is still going to be too challenging.
I’m not sure we have the time to collect all this extra data right now.
And what about the role of the researchers?
Tom: Well, we are also going to be working closely with researchers, who will help collect the data from patients after they have been treated.
Sienna: As far as I’m concerned, they should interview the patients before and during the trials, so I’m in favour of that.
What about treatments being trialled?
Just because we are doctors, it doesn’t mean we know what drugs are being developed.
Tom: Yes, there are new drugs being developed all the time and that can be challenging.
If you ask me, the hospital has made the right decision to focus on a small number of diseases.
Let me tell you more about how that will work at the meeting later.
Sienna: OK.
That makes sense, I guess.
Well, if you ask me, one good reason for doing clinical trials is the financial benefit.
It’ll allow us to invest in new hospital equipment that we really need right now.
Tom: That’s right.
Of course, we could do with the financial support – the additional money will definitely help us buy those new hospital beds we need, but as far as I am concerned, this is about our patients.
This data which I mentioned before is valuable to understand more about certain diseases and prove whether or not new drugs work effectively.
Sienna: You’re right, Tom.
Tom: Right, well, I won’t keep you any longer, but I’m sure you can see why it is so important to come to the meeting at 4 pm to discuss the changes.
Sienna: Absolutely.
Thanks, Tom.
See you later.

lines.text: Welcome, everyone.
My name’s Marianne.
The topic of my presentation today is conservation development in the UK.
OK, so my presentation is going to be in four parts.
First, I’m going to briefly explain what conservation development is, as some of you may not know.
Next, I’m going to explain the impact of humans on natural habitats.

Then I’ll outline some of the work that conservation organizations do to protect bird habitats, and finally, I shall be suggesting how we can, as individuals, help to protect wildlife by thinking a little more about conservation and making small changes in our gardens.
OK.
So let’s begin with a brief explanation of what conservation development is.
It combines social development, that is, the need to develop land for farming or to build new homes, with protecting the environment and the habitat of wildlife species.

A conservation development project is usually managed and controlled by the owner of the land, for example an individual, a business, the local government or a conservation organization like the RSPB – the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds.
By combining conservation with development, communities can still access the resources they require, but in a way which does not create a harsh environmental impact.
Ok – so now I want to move on to my next point and tell you how natural habitats have been affected.
As I mentioned before, the way we farm our land can affect natural habitats.
This is particularly the case for farmland birds.
Many farmland bird species are small, seed-eating birds.
As a direct result of changes in farming methods and crops grown, bird numbers have declined overall by over 9% since 1980 – and some species have declined by as much as 70%.
Let me tell you why.
There has been an increase in farming crops like corn, and a reduction of farming vegetables, like turnips and carrots.
These birds depend on eating seeds from the small plants that were allowed to grow naturally among the vegetable crops.
Now the vegetable crops have been replaced, the plants which the birds relied on for food have almost disappeared.
Because seed-eating birds cannot easily adapt to eating other foods, they have found it particularly difficult to survive in winter when conditions are harsh.
So, how have RSPB’s projects been successful?
Well, they have educated farmers by providing advice about what crops can be introduced to support farmland birds’ natural habitat.
Where it is not possible to completely change the crop, they have suggested small areas of land are left to go wild – that is, not farmed and left for nature to control.
Typically, this might be a metre or two around the edge of a field that is, say, used to grow corn.
Local government has also supported these projects by providing conservation advice.
In addition, farmers who have lost income by changing their farming methods to help protect wildlife can receive financial support.
OK, so you might be thinking that we, as individuals, cannot do much to help wildlife conservation, but this is not the case.
And that brings me to my final point.
How can we help?
Well, if you are lucky enough to have a garden, you can provide birds with fresh drinking water.
This might be a simple birdbath or a small pond which could be used by other water-loving creatures, like frogs.
You could have a wildlife garden.
For example, you could grow plants and flowers which attract bees and other flying insects.
In winter, you can feed birds with seeds, but remember, if you start doing this and attract more birds into your garden, you should keep doing it or they might die.
Right, well, we’re out of time now, but please come and see me later if you would like more information about how you can get involved in wildlife conservation.

lines.text: Presenter: Good afternoon.
Today, we’re joined by Dr Adam Pearson, professor of education.
Recent research has revealed several issues around employing and becoming a qualified Early Years Teacher, or EYT.
That’s a teacher for children up to the age of five, isn’t it?
Dr Adam Pearson: Hello, Simona.
Yes, children who attend nursery school.
There are some barriers to becoming an EYT.

There is a lack of interest among high school graduates to obtain a qualification in this field because it has limited career prospects and it takes around four years to obtain the early years initial teacher training qualification.

This qualification allows graduates to teach children from zero to five years old only, so if they want to teach in schools with older students as their career develops, they will need a further academic qualification.
Most importantly, however, once you obtain a qualification in the field, the job is poorly paid.
Especially when compared to primary or secondary school teachers.
A recent survey found that many early years teachers don’t receive graduate-level pay, with some earning as little as £13,000 per year.
Presenter: What is the reason for that?
Dr Adam Pearson: Mainly it’s because early years teachers don’t get the Qualified Teacher Status, called QTS.
The government says both qualifications, the QTS and the EYT, are equal and should therefore receive the same pay; however, employers don’t see it that way.
Many graduate trainees who go on to acquire EYT status find that whilst they end up with more teaching responsibility, they don’t receive the pay and recognition they deserve.
The EYT is wrongly viewed as a lesser qualification.
Presenter: Do you think the government is doing enough to increase the number of EYTs?
Dr Adam Pearson: Well, the number of EYTs is declining year after year.
As things stand, there are 40 percent fewer EYTs than the government’s target of 2,400.
The government has been criticized for this.
According to our data, for example, just 595 students enrolled on EYT courses in the academic year 2017/2018, even though EYTs had received financial aid to train.
Presenter: What’s your view of the EYT role?
Is it easier to teach the under-fives than say primary- or secondary-aged children?
Dr Adam Pearson: That’s a complex question to answer.
There are a lot of considerations.
How the school is run and managed must be considered together with the student behaviour, whether colleagues are professional, etc.
I’ve visited some nursery schools in, for example, poor areas where the EYT has taken on the role of carer and mentor.
Others have needed more specific skills in teaching very young children with learning difficulties, for example dyslexia or autism.
Often, the schools are underfunded.
Although the EYT does not need to specialize in one subject, they need to be skilled in many.
Presenter: We briefly talked about employers.
What should they be doing differently?
Dr Adam Pearson: Well, the nursery schools are under pressure and I’ll explain why.
I mentioned that often they don’t have much funding.
Obviously, many of the children attending nursery are fee-paying – it’s not a legal requirement for a child to attend school until the age of four, as you know.
Recently, however, the government has introduced 15 hours’ free childcare per week.
That works out at around £7,000 free nursery care per child.
This is great news for parents on lower incomes, but leaves the school with very little to pay its teachers.
This is why many are earning little above the minimum wage.
Presenter: Well, unfortunately, we’ve come to the end of the podcast.
I’d like to thank Dr Pearson for sharing the results of the research and highlighting just how important early years teachers are.
Join me next time for Science in the City.

lines.text: Presenter: Good afternoon.
I’m joined today by climate change author Rachael Greenacre.
We’re talking about planting trees.
Why trees?
Rachael: Hello, Jeremy.
Trees use the carbon dioxide that we humans produce, which is the main gas heating the planet and causing global warming.
Many people, me included, see planting more trees as one possible solution to the problem of climate change.
Presenter: Right.
I understand the government, in an effort to support green initiatives, has promised to plant millions of trees per year.
That’s quite a large number …

Rachael: You are right that the government is supporting green initiatives, but the number of trees they want to plant, around 30 million, is in fact lower than other countries which have programmes in place to plant billions.
Presenter: Why is this such a popular idea?
Rachael: Well, in addition to looking beautiful, forests have practical benefits.
They support wildlife, of course, and hold back flood water.
This is especially important with the increasing storms we are experiencing as a result of global warming.
What’s more, trees provide wood which has a broad range of uses, from building and construction materials to paper and oils used in paints.
As I already mentioned, trees help clean the air by absorbing carbon dioxide.
They take in around 20 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year when we include the additional 30 million trees the government has promised to plant.
Presenter: This sounds good on paper, but I imagine the decision isn’t popular with everyone.
Rachael: No, there are problems, Jeremy.
There’s the question of where to plant a new forest.
If they are planted where crops are grown or where animals are being raised, then some sort of payment would be necessary for the farmer who owns the land.
It could take decades before the farmer might expect to make any sort of profit from a new forest.
Then there’s the problem of planting.
I have watched experienced tree planters planting trees at a rate of one every four seconds, which equals around three to four thousand trees a day.
They are actually more efficient than the machines that can do the same job.
Unfortunately, it isn’t a popular job in this country, so finding labour might be difficult unless we employ experts from overseas.
Presenter: Are those the only challenges?
Rachael: No.
As I mentioned earlier, trees grow slowly, but not only that – young trees, or saplings, require lots of care.
They are affected by extreme changes in the weather, diseases and insects.
Many die before they reach maturity.
This brings me to another issue.
Trees can only use significant amounts of carbon dioxide once they reach the age of around 30 years, so the benefits to the environment are not going to happen quickly.

I said before that we can use trees for wood, but if a tree dies and is left in the ground, all the carbon the tree absorbed when it was alive is released back into the earth and therefore the atmosphere.
Presenter: What can we do about those issues?
Rachael: The key to success is good land management so the young trees have the best possible chance of surviving until they reach maturity.
Let me tell you more about how we can help young trees to reach the age of 30 years.
For instance, we can attach instruments to tree trunks, which measure how fast the tree is growing and how healthy it is.
We can also make sure we plant more than one species of tree.
This means that if one species were lost because of a specific disease, the other might survive.
Also, we should not forget trees require water, and some species more than others.
While a newly planted forest might protect one local community from flooding, it might leave a neighbouring community without enough drinking water.
We must remember this is a long-term plan, so we need long-term goals; otherwise we’re going to fail.
Presenter: Very interesting, Rachael.
We must stop there, I’m afraid, as we’re out of time.
Thank you for joining us today.

lines.text: Rae: And this is the space for our new leisure centre.
What do you think, Jenny?
Jenny: It’s an amazing space, with great potential.
I can’t believe how much has happened since I’ve been away.
I’ve got a million questions.
Are the architects working on the planning yet?
Rae: Yes, we have two firms working on different aspects of the project now.
One is focusing on giving the internal spaces a new lease of life, the other on the outside landscaping.
Here, let me show you how the internal plan is looking.
Jenny: Great!
What are you doing with this space on the plan here?
Maybe we could have an open-plan design.
Rae: Quite a bit.
As you can see, it’s more like a prison than an office in its current form.
We need to open it up so we can create more light.
Look at these internal walls.
We intend to knock them down, as they are about to collapse, and we are also going to raise the roof in the far-right corner so that we can introduce a large skylight.
This will allow both light and fresh air into the space.
Jenny: Wow.
It’s ambitious, isn’t it?
If I’ve understood correctly, this is a conservation area, so the designs need to be sustainable.
There are rules and regulations we’ll need to follow and that takes time.
We won’t be able to cut corners when it comes to the design in order to get things done quicker.
Rae: You’re right.
Well, both architects we are using specialize in sustainable construction and we have instructed them that we want to achieve a development that is sympathetic to the existing area.
They’re not cheap, of course, but they are experts in their field, and once the development is complete, it’ll be a potential gold mine, attracting both local and national businesses to the area.
Let’s take a look outside.
Jenny: Wow, what a beautiful setting.
The last time I was here it was an absolute mess, but now the land’s been cleared, we can really see how it might be transformed.
That lake there and the way the land slopes towards those trees is stunning.
I really think we should have a restaurant with an outdoor terrace on the water’s edge.
It would be a fantastic addition.
Rae: That was our intention, but since you have been away, things have got a bit controversial.
I was told by senior management that the lake is in fact the habitat for a rare species of frog!
Jenny: Oh, I see.
I’m guessing there are serious challenges to overcome.
Rae: Yes, there are a few.
Firstly, we won’t be able to obtain permission to build within 100 metres of the frog’s habitat, which means we need to think about other options.
It’s going to be extremely challenging for me to get the existing plans revised within the timescale we have in mind.
Jenny: That’s terrible!
You must be concerned after all your hard work.
I know you had high hopes for that area in particular.
And, time is money, isn’t it?
Any delay is going to mean that we will lose potential profits.
Rae: Absolutely, but we must take care of the wildlife.
So, although changing the design is controversial and we may lose money, we need to go back to the drawing board on this part of the project.
We will have to think again about the lakeside development completely.
Jenny: Wouldn’t it be better if we turned the lake into a wildlife conservation area?
Not only could we protect the frogs’ habitat, but we could also encourage species of birds and insects into the area.
That could be an excellent feature for bringing tourists to the development.
Rae: That is exactly what I was thinking, Jenny.
Let’s discuss it a bit further.

lines.text: Interviewer: Well, we all know non-renewable energy sources are declining and most of us have heard about solar, wind and hydro energy, but what about the power of algae?
I’m joined today by Dr Tandy Millen, researcher at Reedman University.
Dr Tandy, what is algae and how do we get energy from it?
Dr Tandy Millen: Hello, Kyle.
Algae are a group of very small plants found in water.
These simple plants use a process called photosynthesis – basically photosynthesis is how plants generate energy from sunlight.
This process allows algae to make carbohydrates, proteins and oils which in turn can be changed to plant-based fuel, biofuel.
By the way, this is almost the same process that humans and animals get energy from the sun, too.
Interviewer: That’s very interesting.
Algae are marine plants that are a food source for fish and other marine animals like whales, I believe.
But, don’t you think it would be easier to leave them as a food source?
Dr Tandy Millen: As you’ve just said, algae are consumed by marine animals, especially whales in huge quantities.
What’s more, in 2013 researchers also found algae in the stomachs of sharks.
It’s often thought that sharks only eat meat, but this data shows that sharks consume algae because of its high mineral content.
However, algae have so many other uses beyond being a food source.
Interviewer: Let’s go back to fuel.
You mentioned algae can be turned into plant-based fuel, biofuel.
What is that exactly?
Dr Tandy Millen: Well, biofuel is any fuel that comes from a plant or algae material or from animal waste – which can be a very efficient energy source.
Interviewer: I would imagine you’d need a lot of algae to, say, power a city.
For this reason, I think that an energy project like this would be too ambitious.
Dr Tandy Millen: Well, I agree it might not be straightforward; however, converting algae into energy through biofuel is an increasingly popular form of renewable energy.
Some argue that it is one of the best solutions for the decline of our natural resources.
This is due to the speed at which algae grow – they are one of the fastest-growing plants on the planet.
Interviewer: That sounds great.
You also need to consider where and how algae could be grown.
I expect farmed algae would need a lot of maintenance.
Dr Tandy Millen: Yes.
That’s right.
There are a number of elements to consider.
For example, there are massive costs involved in farming, harvesting and converting the algae into fuel.
So, although algae are fast-growing and large volumes can be farmed at once, there are cost drawbacks.
Another interesting point is that algae can help to clean water by absorbing and removing poisonous substances that are harmful for humans to consume.
Interviewer: I never knew that.
By and large, I see what you’re saying, but other sources of energy, like solar panels, just seem more efficient.
I’m not sure algae as an energy source are a viable option for future generations.
Dr Tandy Millen: Well, it’s going to be a challenge, I won’t deny it.
We need to overcome the drawbacks around expense, for one thing, but trust me when I say, even with limitations it has huge potential.
Interviewer: Thank you, Dr Tandy.
I’m afraid that’s all we have time for.
Join me next week for a discussion on a further interesting source.

lines.text: Presenter: Good morning.
We’ve seen the recent story in the press about the controversial decision by Drayfield Hospital to spend more than £25,000 on artwork for the new children’s ward.
This decision has produced a number of strong reactions from the general public, and today I am joined by three of our listeners who have different opinions about it.
Welcome, Sonya.
How do you feel about this decision?
Sonya: Good morning, Tony.
It’s outrageous!
If we waste the money on this art, the health service will be under even more pressure.
There’s never any spare money for our health service.
Surely it would be far better to spend it on providing care for patients and not on art displays that would be better in an art gallery.
Presenter: That’s a valid point, Sonya.
But isn’t art supposed to have health benefits?
I’d like to welcome Miranda, who I understand is a street artist, to join the debate – I hope that’s the right term, Miranda.
Miranda: Hi, Tony.
Yes, that’s correct.
A number of studies on hospital patients have shown that art therapy improves anxiety and reduces pain.
In my opinion, it’s appropriate to spend £25,000 on artwork with those results.
In today’s world where everyone is stressed at work and under pressure, we need art therapy more than ever.
In fact, I’d suggest spending more if the budget allowed.
Presenter: So, it’s money well spent.
Good morning, Rosie.
What’s your view on this?
Your daughter is in Drayfield Hospital at the moment.
I hope she’s doing well.
Rosie: Hello, Tony.
Yes, thank you – she’ll be home next week.
Right, well, I’m not sure, to be honest.
I understand the figure in question is a small percentage of their overall budget.
Presenter: Yes, the overall budget is £10 million according to the official report.
Rosie: Right, and I was there last week when they put the artwork up.
Some of the contemporary pieces are quite stunning.
I love it – I just wonder if children of that age are too young to really appreciate the expensive art they are looking at.
Presenter: That’s a good point.
Miranda, how would you respond to that?

Miranda: I hear what Rosie is saying about age and that’s true in some ways, but it’s not simply about art appreciation in the traditional sense; it’s also about communicating with young people and doing that through self-expression.
Presenter: So, you’re saying that art can be a method of communication?
Miranda: Yes, artists communicate their attitudes, emotions and even personalities through their art, which is why art is so diverse and personal.
Self-expression and creativity are very important for teenagers as it teaches them that everyone is different—
Sonya: May I say something here, Tony?
Presenter: Well, perhaps you could just let Miranda finish, Sonya, and then you can have your say.
You were saying, Miranda?
Miranda: Yes.
I was getting to the point of art criticism.
Children, in this case those in the hospital ward, like Rosie’s daughter, are art critics of the work the hospital has displayed.
By considering the value of the art around them, children make decisions about what really matters to them.
That is a positive thing, especially at a time when they are unwell.
Presenter: Thank you, Miranda.
Very thought-provoking.
Sonya?
Sonya: No offence to Miranda, but what is all this nonsense about self-expression?
I was shopping in town last week and the amount of graffiti everywhere was terrible.
Most of it is done illegally, I might add.
Art has its place and that is either at school or university, or in art galleries.
I’m afraid my mind is made up on that point.
Presenter: Well, I’m afraid we have run out of time.
As you can see, this is a controversial decision by Drayfield Hospital, which I’m sure we’ll continue to debate.

lines.text: Ben: Hey, Mia.
That was an interesting lecture about retirement options and whether it is better to retire or keep working under the new state pension law.
Mia: Hey, Ben.
Yes, it was.
It’s only right that older people now have the choice to work longer.
Just working one extra year can increase a person’s pension fund by up to £4,500, the data said.
Ben: Yes, and that’s not all.
If everyone over 65 chose to work for an extra 12 months, GDP – that’s gross domestic product – would increase by one percent.
That doesn’t sound like a lot, but it’s equal to £16 billion for the economy.
What do you think, Tom?
Tom: I understand the argument, Ben, but where are all these jobs coming from?
For me, there aren’t enough jobs for the younger generation these days.
Surely, it’s the responsibility of the younger generation to devote some time to taking care of their older relatives.
That way, they can relax and enjoy their retirement.
Mia: Tom, you assume that those who have reached retirement age want to give up work.
I know what you mean about the younger generation having responsibility for their parents or grandparents as they get older, but isn’t what you’re saying unfair towards elderly people?
Forcing people to retire at 55 may have made sense in the 1950s, but ideas and lifestyles were different from the way they are now in the 21st century.
Ben: That’s a valid point, Mia.
Thirty percent of today’s workers are over the age of 50, and 1 million are over 65.
The number of people who continue to work at retirement age increased by almost 300,000 between 2011 and 2014 and the trend is growing year on year.
How can anyone say that the elderly don’t have a huge role to play in our economy?
If someone wants to carry on working and using their skills, it’s quite right they should be able to.
In some cases, they have a lot more knowledge than the younger generation, who can learn from them.
Tom: I take your point, Ben, but people at retirement age, for example, haven’t got the skills required for the majority of today’s jobs which involve computers, etcetera.
They weren’t brought up in a technological age like we were.
I don’t think it would be fair to put someone in a role they weren’t skilled for just because they’re older – that wouldn’t be fair for the more highly skilled younger people.
We need to ensure that people get jobs if they have the right skills.
Mia: That’s nonsense.
Just because someone is older than 50, it doesn’t mean they are afraid of technology or unskilled in that area.
I get your point that the older generation may not have had a smartphone all their lives, but there has been a clear increase in the number of people over 55 owning a smartphone.
In 2019, 55% of people aged over 55 owned one according to one survey.
That number is significant.
What’s more, for the first time ever, more women aged 60 to 64 are in work than not in work, according to analysis of data from the Office for National Statistics.
Ben: Yes, I read that.
The number of older women in work has increased by 51% since the government changed the state pension age.
Interestingly, the number of working men aged between 60 and 64 increased by only 13% over the same period.
Mia: Working is a positive choice for older people, as it gives them financial independence.
Personally, I think it’s about choice.
Age is, or should be, irrelevant.

lines.text: Good afternoon.
It’s great to see you all here today.
I’m Sandy Dickenson and I’m going to focus on three important construction innovations.

Before we begin, however, I’d just like to mention that my company, Innovators Construct, will be at next week’s architectural design conference in London where I’ll be launching our energy-saving under-floor heating product.
Please do come along to the event if you can.
Right, so let’s get started.
First, I’d like to talk to you about a concept called ‘digital twins’.
A digital twin is basically a computer-made copy of an asset which can be an object, a system or a process.
It uses a computer program that takes real-world data about the asset and predicts how that data will affect the asset.
This means that the digital twin can show us how the asset will perform without the need to test it in the real world.
How can the digital twin help construction projects?
Well, it can include all the information from design through to construction and then operation.
Because the digital twin can analyze data as it arrives, it helps project managers to make early decisions and avoid unexpected costs.
Or, if additional costs are necessary, it allows project managers to remain in control throughout the cycle of the project.
The digital twin was implemented for the Thames Estuary Flood Management Project where it analyzed 70 years of historical data.
By getting data up to 25 years faster than other more historical methods, it transformed the way developers and architects work together.
Next, I want to talk to you about augmented reality.
Augmented reality technology has come a long way since it was invented in 1968 by Ivan Sutherland.
He was a computer graphics engineer as well as a teacher, and he developed the first augmented reality display system with the help of his students.
Augmented reality technologies, like ‘smart glasses’, give you an interactive experience that mixes the real world with a computer-made one.
For example, this means you can look at a house that is being built right now, but the glasses can show you what it will look like when it is finished.
It is a three-dimensional, or 3D, example of reality and is quite amazing.
Using AR technology, we can put the potential customers directly inside a building at the design stage.
Furthermore, when working onsite, engineers wearing ‘smart glasses’ see where there are electrical wires hidden behind walls.
The AR technology, in this example, would act as a safety or alarm system.
Finally, I want to talk about robots.
For many of us, robots are a thing of films – most of us have seen R2-D2 or C-3PO in George Lucas’ Star Wars.
These lovable robots, with different personalities and behaviours, were – and still are – popular with cinema fans today.
Robots are already in use today within the construction industry, in a range of shapes and sizes.
They can lay bricks, move materials and 3D-print among other things.
However, the way of the future is ‘swarm robotics’, a new, experimental technology that is developing very fast.
What is swarm robotics?
Simply put, swarm robotics is a multi-robot system which consists of a large number of simple individual robots.
Think of it like a family of bees, called a swarm, that work individually but for the benefit of the whole family.
One of the advantages of swarm robotics is that it can be designed to work on large-scale projects, and they are a self-organizing network, making them extremely efficient.
Several companies have started working on the next stage of robots and robot networks, which is the development of mobility – the ability to move from one place to another.

This is positive news for architecture, design and construction industries as the ability to use robots on rough ground, which is hilly or rocky, for example, would be a huge step forward from where we are now.
Right.
Well, that’s all we have time for today.
I think you’ll agree from these innovations that this is by far the most exciting time to be involved in the construction industry as a developer, engineer or architect.
Thank you.
Now, any questions?

lines.text: Presenter: Good morning, and welcome to this morning’s podcast, The Rise of the Social Seniors.
I’m joined today by psychologist Dr Aneka Andrews.
So, are the elderly taking over social media websites, like Facebook and Twitter, Dr Andrews?
Dr Andrews: Good morning, Charlie.
I wouldn’t say taking over exactly, but they are starting to use smartphones and tablets in record numbers.
Presenter: But surely, social media is a little challenging for older people.
Wouldn’t they be better off leaving all that to the younger generation?
Dr Andrews: Charlie!
Why on earth would you suggest that?
A quarter of the over-75s use tablets, and why shouldn’t they?
There are huge cognitive and mental health benefits to this growing trend.
Presenter: Yes.
The older generation certainly enjoy online brain training quizzes, and crosswords.
Dr Andrews: That’s not really what I was referring to.
What I’m talking about are things like setting up a social media account.
Think about it, Charlie, learning a new skill can be challenging.
For example, you need to focus.
You need to navigate in an unknown world.
You need to acquire new knowledge to do things like set up a profile, upload a photograph or post a status update.
For someone born in 1945 this might stimulate the brain in the same way as going to school or learning to speak a new language.
Presenter: If I felt like I had to go back to school, I don’t think I’d bother.
Seriously, though, it might be an idea if they did go back, I mean to college or do some sort of computer training course.
Dr Andrews: It’s interesting you say that.
Did you know that a UK study has shown that using social media actually improves the health of senior citizens?
In the study, 100 people aged over 65 were studied over a period of two years.
Some received computer training, for example, on how to use the internet while the other group did not.
Those who surfed the web experienced an improvement in their mental and physical abilities.
In contrast, these abilities declined steadily for the other group.
Presenter: That’s remarkable.
I hadn’t realized elderly people were so confident online.
Dr Andrews: Ah, don’t misunderstand me, Charlie.
I didn’t say they were all confident.
While the older generation are increasingly active online, some do lack online confidence.
A fifth of over 65s do not describe themselves as confident online.
This is particularly the case when managing personal data.
For instance, one in five internet users over the age of 65 said they were not confident about managing passwords and other sensitive data.
More worryingly, perhaps, 16 percent of users over 55 admitted to never considering the privacy of their online posts.
That is the largest percentage for any age group.
Presenter: What about getting guidance from grandchildren about online safety?
Dr Andrews: I guess that might work if they have grandchildren that they see face to face or online on a regular basis, but we need to think about a more practical approach.
Some websites offer practical information, but that’s only helpful if people know it’s there and how to find it.
Presenter: Yes, websites can be difficult to understand when they are describing something technical.
So how do you think the issue of online safety should be approached?
Dr Andrews: In my view, the only answer is a more proactive approach, where agencies step in to provide support if relatives are unable to do so for whatever reason.
Especially as we are seeing more cybercrime daily that targets elderly people.
That way, the older generation can continue to enjoy the health benefits with confidence.
Presenter: Thank you, Dr Andrews.
Cybercrime will be the topic of our podcast next week.
For now, that’s all we have time for.
Thank you.
